decision.reason: A correlação é sustentada por Interact6–7 e OP11–13, mas pergunta e resposta repetem substancialmente article-39adb0cfa84e-57, já existente nesta ampliação: as mesmas duas recompensas condicionadas versus desbloqueios opcionais. Requer um nexo distinto para entregar uma questão nova substantiva. Sugestão: contrastar Task-based Rewards com scaffolding/tutoriais e domínio gradual de ferramentas de World Creation, mantendo limites e evidências completas.

card.question: Como Task-based Rewards e Ad-locked Rewards podem ser comparados aos desbloqueios opcionais de World Creation sem declarar toda recompensa um padrão enganoso?
card.answer: O Interact descreve missões além do fluxo principal e visualização obrigatória de anúncios para obter benefícios como casos de Forced Action. Operationalizing admite [[desbloqueios opcionais por participação significativa]], preservando um [[núcleo criativo acessível]], sem pagamento ou grind excessivo como barreira às funções fundamentais. A comparação exige perguntar o que é condicionado, quão essencial é o benefício e se a atividade sustenta escolha e domínio, em vez de apenas observar que existe recompensa. Trata-se de contraste analítico entre descrições de apps e critérios de um padrão em jogos. O Interact não mede a frustração de necessidades dos jogadores, e os exemplos de World Creation não constituem prova de eficácia ou viabilidade comercial.

We did not find any statistically significant difference in any app category. Di
Geronimo and Hidaka also failed the test and did not find any correlations
between the number of DPs and the app categories. This test supports the
hypothesis of the pervasive nature of DPs. A Kruskal-Wallis test ( χ

< .001) revealed a significant difference between the DP subclasses. A Dwass-
Steel-Critchlow-Fligner pairwise comparisons showed that the Nagging subclass
is significantly higher than all other subclasses, except when comparing to Forced
Action (W = -5.6466, p = 0.008).
Our findings also revealed six DP cases previously unreported in international
research. They demonstrate novel applications of known DPs: (i) “ Terms/Policy
in Another Language ” (Untranslation case) when crucial information for the
user (terms of service or privacy policy) is in another language, even if the app
is in the native user language, creating a barrier between the user and the in-
formation; (ii) “ Terms/Policy Out of Bounds ” (Obstruction case) redirects
the user to an external page, typically a web page, to access the terms of service
or privacy policy, increasing unnecessary stress and reducing the likelihood of
reading; (iii) “ Ads with layers ” (Obstruction case) specifies chains of multiple
time-delayed sub-ads to extend user exposure within the same content, making
more than one “attention call” in the same time span; (iv) “ Task-based Re-
wards ” (Forced Action case) describes cases where the app presents a mission
beyond the main flow, that when completed rewards the user with some aspect
of the app services; (v) “ Ad-locked Rewards ” (Forced Action case) indicates
when the user is forced to watch an advertisement to receive a reward like vir-
tual coins, time accelerators, or other bonuses; (vi) “ Evoke Emotions to Take
Action ” (Toying with Emotions case) specifies uses of any language or other
appealing visual elements to persuade the user into an action. Those DP cases
occur 158 times in our classification, accounting for approximately 21% of the
751 DPs found presenting specific occurrences of: Terms/Policy in Another Lan-
guage (45 times); Terms/Policy Out of Bounds (26 times); Ads with Layers (42

It’s Like a Dark Patterns Paradise 7

times); Task-based Rewards (20 times); Ad-locked Rewards (14 times); Evoke
Emotions to Take Action (11 times).
Real-world examples of each of the new DP cases are available in the study’s
database on Zenodo [16].

4 Discussions

The discovery of six new cases of dark patterns, which constitute approximately
21% of the reported DPs, provides a more specific and consistent classification
of these patterns. This new classification aligns the previous list of DP cases
more closely with the Brazilian context. Additionally, it suggests that apps in
Brazil (whether local or international) are employing innovative strategies to
discourage usage and prompt users to take action, beyond merely displaying ads
or pop-ups. These strategies often involve creating new tasks that engage users
in activities beneficial to the developer, such as enabling notifications for app
updates or using persuasive messages to encourage users to rate the app.
Our results indicate that the presence of DPs in Brazilian apps aligns closely
with those in American apps, with an average score of 7.51 compared to Di
Geronimo’s 7.4, and a prevalence of 96% versus Di Geronimo’s 95%. However,
the distribution of these results in the DP subclasses differentiates these two
scenarios. When analyzing the most recurring subclasses, it is interesting to
note that even though Nagging is in first place in both surveys, Brazilian apps
stand out in the percentage difference (34,5%).
A broader perspective on this distribution difference reveals that in Brazil,
apps often use DPs that aim to manipulate users by directing them to alternative
activities, while in the US, they tend to manipulate users by tricking them into
making specific decisions and taking certain actions. The three most common
DPs tried to obstruct or force the user to interact with the application. Therefore,
there is an increase in the number of cases involving Nagging and Forced Action
in the Brazilian context. Moreover, the fourth most common is Untranslation
(Linguistic Dead-Ends), appearing at least once in 45% of the apps.
However, when comparing our results with Hidaka’s findings [20], we found
an increase in presence per app on 10 out of the 16 subclasses considered in the
analyses. This suggests that the Japanese DP situation appears to be handled
more strictly compared to the Brazilian one. This could be due to cultural, le-
gal, and market differences. Further, the subclasses with the most increase were
Aesthetic Manipulation (171,40%), Unstranslation (100%) and Trick Question
(100%). The most decrease being Hidden Information (-116,60%), Roach Motal
(-100%), and Intermediate Currency (-60%). Furthermore, the substantial in-
crease in the Unstranslation subclass in the Brazilian context draws attention
to a misuse of language that intentionally obscures information by utilizing a
foreign language, even when the rest of the app is in the user’s native language.
Those differences, particularly the Untranslation, should be addressed in future
works about DPs in Brazil, since the population has a score considered low in
proficiency tests such as the EF English Proficiency Index [4].

Name World Creation

Problem Addresses limited player agency, creativity, and

expression in pre-defined game worlds.

Context Digital games (sandbox, platformers, creative

suites) allowing player interaction with systems

and others.

Proposed Solution Provides accessible tools for players to create,

customize, collaborate, and share scenarios

without core functions depending on payment or

excessive grind.

Avoiding Decrease in
SDT Needs

Autonomy: Player control over creations.

Competence: Mastery of tools, creative achieve-
ment.

Relatedness: Sharing, collaboration,

experiencing others’ content.

Watch For Gating core tools behind payment/grind; poorly

designed/obfuscated tools; restrictive sharing;

insufficient scaffolding for complex tools.

Implementation
Examples
(Failing/Matching)

Failing: Core tools paywalled/grind-locked;

buggy tools.

Matching: Accessible core suite; intuitive tools;

easy sharing.

Good Examples LittleBigPlanet (Create Mode), Super Mario
Maker , Dreams .

dependencies on direct payment or excessive repetitive grinding for core creative

functions.

Avoiding Decrease in Autonomy, Relatedness, and Competence

Autonomy - World Creation promotes autonomy by giving players plenty of

control and freedom (the autonomy to customize their own environments) over

their creations and their interaction with the game world. It prevents reducing

autonomy by definition.

Competence - The pattern enables players to learn, master tools, be creative,

and overcome design challenges (harnessing their creativity, sense of ‘accomplish-
ment’). Successfully creating and sharing content builds a sense of competence. It

prevents a loss of competence by offering the opportunity for skill development.

Relatedness - Being able to share creations, collaborate, or play others’ work

(share these creations and invite other players to join, encouraging social inter-
action) satisfies relatedness needs. Facilitating social connection through collab-
orative, creative activities helps prevent a decrease in relatedness.

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 123

Watch For. A properly designed World Creation pattern would go out of its

way not to make fundamental creative tools conditional on excessive grinding or

direct payment. These are predicted risks for psychological harm (frustration,

exploitation) and are set patterns that necessarily thwart autonomy (loss of

liberty to create) and competence (progress feels hindered or artificial). The

bottom line for maintaining the World Creation framework as an RP is that

fundamental creative tools, basic elements, and the main ability to save and

share creations should not be expressly limited by financial constraints or only

provided through substituting payment for excessive grind. Monetization should

target optional enhancements, platform access, or adjacent community offerings,

all while keeping the basic act of creation separate and proficiency-dependent,

without creating financial pressure as a barrier to core activity.

Example of Implementations

Implementations Failing to Meet RP Criteria

To gate key components , required mechanisms, or the storage and sharing

of works behind boring, repetitive gameplay cycles (grind) or outright financial

expenditure. Imposing costs on essential tools would directly hinder autonomy,

as players are unable to realize their creative vision and competence freely, given

that the capacity to construct is unjustly restricted by external factors unrelated

to creative ability.

Poor implementations or Obfuscated Tools. The presentation of creation

tools that are poorly designed, buggy, lack basic features (like precise positioning

or undo functions), or are poorly documented undermine the player’s feeling of

competency, making them feel hampered in their ability to realize their ideas

because of limitations imposed by the tools instead of limitations imposed by

their skill level. Additionally, this reduces autonomy by rendering specific forms

of creative expression effectively impossible.

Restrictive Sharing and Discovery Mechanisms. When sharing works is

difficult, discovery of the works of others is inadequately supported (e.g., no

search/curation), or there are arbitrary restrictions on what or how much can

be shared, the relatedness dimension of the pattern is strongly negated. This can

be annoying, as many creators’ motivations include sharing and communicating

with the community. Restricting this diminishes the value of creation.

Insufficient Scaffolding of Sophisticated Tools. Very sophisticated creation

environments can overwhelm users if not backed up by solid tutorials, progres-
sive feature unlocking, or overt guidance (scaffolding). Unveiling tremendous

complexity without help can consistently lead to frustration and abandonment,

precluding competence.

Implementations In line with RP Criteria

Accessible Core Creative Suite. To make a robust set of core creation

elements and tools immediately available to the player. Though some extra

pieces may be gated behind an upfront barrier, the core capacity for creation

124 L. S. Filho and T. Darin

and expression is untethered from unreasonable grinding or monetary expenses.

This strongly encourages autonomy and establishes a foundation for competency

development.

Intuitive Design and Clear Feedback. Offering user-friendly, responsive

tools with clear feedback and adequate tutorials (integrated into the gameplay

itself) gives players a sense of empowerment. This directly supports competence

by making the tools learnable and usable and minimizing frustration with the

interface.

Facilitating Sharing and Community. Emphasize being able to post and

discover/play community content easily. Making sharing and discovery easy and

satisfying enhances the entire creative ecosystem and avoids the frustrating trend

of isolating creators. This might include sharing full games and experiences.

Optional Unlocks By Engaging Play. While fundamental tools ought to be

readily available, providing optional cosmetic qualities, upgraded parts, or the-
matic elements as rewards for participation in many of the game’s aspects (which

do not solely revolve around grinding) might suit the RP model. This would pro-
vide room for progress objectives without restricting required creativity, perhaps

augmenting players’ senses of competence as they acquire fresh creative possi-
bilities.

Good Examples. The LittleBigPlanet game franchise has a “Create Mode”

that allows players to create levels using tools provided by the developers. These

levels can be accessed by other players if they are published to the community.

Similarly, the Super Mario Maker franchise allows players to create levels using

items and resources from other games in the Mario franchise (Fig. 1 ). Dreams

goes even further, allowing players to create entire games and experiences, both

visually and musically.

Fig. 1. Super Mario Maker as an example of World Creation Pattern.

card.question: Como distinguir uma missão externa condicionada por recompensa, descrita como Task-based Rewards, de uma tarefa de aprendizagem que oferece scaffolding em World Creation?
card.answer: No Interact, [[Task-based Rewards apresenta uma missão além do fluxo principal]] cuja conclusão recompensa o usuário com algum aspecto do serviço. Em World Creation, Operationalizing discute outro papel para atividades e orientação: [[tutoriais, apresentação gradual de funcionalidades e feedback claro]] ajudam a tornar ferramentas criativas complexas aprendíveis e utilizáveis. A síntese exige examinar a função da tarefa: ela apoia o domínio da própria criação ou desloca o usuário para uma ação condicionada ao benefício? Não basta chamar a atividade de tutorial, nem pressupor que toda missão ou progressão seja enganosa. O texto também adverte que complexidade sem apoio pode dificultar competência; isso é diferente de impor uma tarefa externa como condição. A comparação articula descrições e critérios de design, sem afirmar que os estudos testaram conjuntamente essa distinção ou mediram efeitos causais sobre autonomia, competência e bem-estar.
